op.label: {before} → {after}

cq.fingerprint_same: {v2} and {v1} have the same fingerprint ({fp}): one computation with two names, one copy of the state.
cq.fingerprint_differs: Two computations: {v1} has fingerprint {left} and {v2} has {right}. Each holds its own state; dropping one leaves the other running.
cq.computation_unknown: Whether this would share {v1}'s computation cannot be told here: a plan is missing.
cq.separate: The plans differ, so the fingerprints will too: registered, this version is a computation of its own, filling its own state from its sources. {v1} keeps running untouched.
cq.may_share: The plans are identical. Registered with {v1}'s keys ({keys}) and retention ({retention}) it would share {v1}'s computation — one state, two names — unless a row filter differs between the two registrations. Other keys or retention make it a second computation. The fingerprint the engine answers with settles it; {v1}'s is {fp}.
cq.may_share_drafts: The plans are identical: registered with the same keys and retention, the two would be one computation.
cq.schema_unknown: The output columns cannot be compared: a side does not validate, or validation is unavailable.
cq.schema_same: The output columns are the same, with the same types.
cq.schema_reordered: The same columns in another order ({before} → {after}): a client reading by position sees them move.
cq.schema_changes: Output columns: {changes}. A client that reads the view by column name sees the difference.
cq.keys_available: {v1}'s key ({keys}) is in this version's output: it can be keyed the same way, and a point query by that key works on both.
cq.keys_missing: {v1}'s key column {missing} is not in this version's output: it cannot be keyed as {v1} is, and a point query by that key would have nothing to look up.
cq.state_same: The state has the same shape: the stateful operators are unchanged.
cq.state_changes: The state changes shape — {changes} — so none of {v1}'s state could serve this version.
cq.not_determinable: Not determinable here: how long this version takes to fill, and how much state it will hold. The engine does not estimate either before registration.

landing.lede: A query you register is a question the engine keeps answering. Not a job you submit and wait on — a view that is already correct when you read it, maintained row by row as the data arrives, and shared by everyone who asked the same thing.

name.title: pravāha — that which flows
name.p1_flow: : a river's flow, continuous and directional. Not the water, which is always different water — the
name.p1_after: , which is the thing that persists.
name.p2: Which is what a stream is, and what makes streaming hard to reason about. The rows are gone the moment they pass. What you keep is the answer they changed, and the discipline is knowing which answers a row can still change and which it cannot.
name.p3_question: can anything still arrive that changes this?
name.p3_after: — is what watermarks answer, what retention rests on, and what decides when a window may close.

different.incremental_body: A change is a delta. Z-sets carry weights, so a correction is a retraction and an insert — never a rescan.
different.event_time_body: A window closes when the data says it is over, not when the clock does. Late rows correct the answer rather than being lost.
different.shared_body: Two people asking the same question get one computation and one copy of the state — matched on the normalised plan, not the SQL text.
different.bounded_body: Every operator that could grow without limit has a bound, and a query with no bound is refused at plan time rather than at 3am.

does.continuous_body: Register SQL under a name. The engine maintains its view for as long as it is registered, and clients read or subscribe.
does.joins_body: Two streams joined on a key and a time bound — including LEFT, where the unmatched row is emitted once the window has passed.
does.protocol_body: Arrow Flight SQL for query, prepare, register and subscribe. Both SDKs and the CLI speak it; so does any Flight client.
does.answers_body: A view is already computed when you ask. There is no serving database because the serving database is not needed.

diagram.title: How Pravaha works
diagram.desc: Rows from your stores feed declared streams. A continuous query, registered once, turns every change into a Z-set delta and maintains a keyed view. The view is read by key, subscribed to commit by commit, or written to a sink. Checkpoints and the registry journal let a restart resume.

l.or_captured_from_a_change: or captured from a change log
l.one_cut_across_every_input: one cut across every input · a restart resumes, it does not replay from scratch

how.1: A stream is declared — its schema, which column is event time, how late its rows may arrive — and bound to a source plugin that reads one of your stores.
how.2: A continuous query is registered once, under a name and a key. Calcite parses and plans it; Pravaha's own operators run it, as generated code, on a lane — and identical questions share one computation.
how.3: Every row becomes a change with a weight: +1 for a row appearing, −1 for one withdrawn. Operators transform changes into changes, so the work is proportional to what changed.
how.4: The watermark — how far event time has certainly advanced — closes windows. A late row inside the allowed lateness reopens a window as a retraction of the old answer and the corrected one, in one commit.
how.5: The view is the answer, maintained and keyed. Applications read it by key over Flight SQL or the PostgreSQL wire protocol, subscribe to its commits, or have the node write each commit to a sink. Checkpoints cut every input at one point, so a restart resumes.

guides.lede: The long-form documents the engine ships with, rendered in place from the repository's docs/ -- the same text a reader of the source sees, so the two cannot drift. Each topic in the help links to the guide behind it.

help.heading: Documentation
help.title: Help
help.blurb: Everything below is available over Flight SQL and both SDKs; nothing requires this console. These pages are markdown files under content/help/, rendered at request time — so they are versioned, reviewable in a pull request alongside the behaviour they describe, and cannot drift from the release that shipped them.

tutorials.heading: Working through Pravaha
tutorials.title: Tutorials
tutorials.blurb: Worked walkthroughs, end to end and with real calls: registering a continuous query and watching it maintained, joining two streams with a time bound, subscribing from both SDKs, and reading the case studies the engine ships with.

login.role_note: Changeable at any time from the account menu. It picks where you land and what the command palette offers first; it grants nothing.
login.gate_note: This gate protects the console's own controls. It is not the engine's identity model — the engine authenticates its clients through the deployment's own provider, and a second, weaker account system beside it would be worse than an honest lock.
login.wrong_password: That is not the console password.

live.lede_before: Every committed change to the view, as the engine publishes it:
live.lede_minus: a row withdrawn. A correction arrives as a withdrawal of the old row and an insert of the new one, so the current rows below are the running sum of both — never a count of messages.
live.noscript_before: Live changes arrive over server-sent events, which need JavaScript. The
live.tap_note: Applied at the engine's tap, so rows you did not ask for never cross the network.
live.rows_note: the view now, plus every change since

dlq.title: Dead letters — {name}
dlq.heading: Records this query could not decode
dlq.retention_title: pravaha.dlq.max-bytes, .max-entries and .max-age. Past the bound the oldest are evicted and counted, never dropped quietly.
dlq.evicted: {n} older entries ({bytes} bytes) have been evicted by retention and are gone. The bound is {bound}: raise pravaha.dlq.max-bytes, or drain the queue more often.
dlq.replay_done: {done} replayed as new rows at the query's current frontier; {again} failed to decode again and went back on the queue.
dlq.semantics: A replayed record is a new row at the query's current frontier, not a rewind: nothing is re-read and no earlier answer is recomputed. A record that fails to decode again goes back on the queue as a new entry rather than being retried.
dlq.choose_one: Choose the dead letter {id} to replay

none.title: {name} has no dead letters
none.body: Every record its sources have sent has decoded. A record that cannot be decoded is written here with its bytes and its reason, and the source reads on.

unconfigured.title: This node keeps no dead letters
unconfigured.body: pravaha.dlq.directory is not set, so a record a source cannot decode stops that source rather than being kept. That is not an empty queue: it is the queue being switched off, and a bad record ends the poll and takes the rest of the feed with it.

error.none_chosen: Choose which dead letters to replay. Replaying a whole queue is not offered: a queue is usually a mix of causes, and most of it is still malformed.

cutover.title: Replacing {name}
cutover.heading: Replacing {name}
cutover.no_eta: There is no estimate and no percentage here, and there will not be one: a source does not say how much history it holds, so there is no total to be a share of. What is below is measured — rows read, the rate, the partitions that have reached the live stream, and how far behind the running version the candidate's event time is.
cutover.candidate_title: The fingerprint of the computation being prepared.
cutover.replacing_title: The fingerprint of the computation serving this name now.

none.title: {name} is not being replaced
none.body: A blue/green replacement runs a new version of this query beside the running one, reads the history its sources still hold, splices onto the live stream where the running version has reached, and waits for you to move the name across. Until you do, the name answers exactly what it answers now.
none.note: The console does not start a replacement from a blank form: the new version is SQL, and SQL is written in the workbench, where the planner refuses what it cannot run before anything is registered.

progress.heading: The backfill
progress.live_rows: Records read from the live stream

rollback.heading: The rollback window
rollback.open: The version this replaced is retained until {until}. Until then, rolling back puts it back.
rollback.open_note: Rolling back ends every subscription to the name, as the cutover did: a reader subscribes again and starts from a fresh snapshot.
rollback.closed_note: The window ran to {until} and the version this replaced is no longer retained. There is nothing to roll back to; going back now means registering the old SQL again and backfilling it.
rollback.over: This replacement is {state}, so there is no window to keep open.
rollback.not_yet: Nothing has been cut over yet, so there is nothing to roll back. A window opens when the name moves to the candidate, and its length is the rollback.retention this replacement was started with.

controls.heading: Controls
controls.cutover_title: Move the name to the candidate, at a position both versions have consumed exactly.
controls.cutover_early: The candidate has not read all of the history yet. Cutting over now is refused by the engine, because the two versions would be at different positions in their input.
controls.rollback_title: Put the replaced version back, while it is still retained.
controls.rollback_gone: The version this replaced is no longer retained, so there is nothing to roll back to.
controls.note: The ceiling may be lowered while the backfill runs and not raised above the one it was started with; the engine refuses a raise rather than the console quietly clamping it. Pause keeps what has been read. Abandon ends a replacement that has not cut over and releases the candidate.

cutover.refused_title: This console's identity may not act on this replacement
cutover.refused_body: Starting, throttling, cutting over and rolling back all need the administer permission on this name, and the engine's policy says: {reason}

confirm.cutover_title: Cut over to the new version of “{name}”?
confirm.cutover_body: Every reader of {name} sees the candidate's answer after this, and every open subscription ends with PRV-4019 and has to subscribe again. The replaced version is kept for the rollback window and no longer.
confirm.rollback_title: Roll “{name}” back to the replaced version?
confirm.rollback_body: Every reader of {name} sees the old answer again after this, and every open subscription ends and has to subscribe again. The candidate is released.

history.heading: Who has served this name
history.not_carried: The engine records who served this name from which seam, and the status this console reads does not carry it. An empty list here would read as “nobody has”, which is a different thing, so nothing is listed.
history.none_title: Nothing has served this name but the version running now
history.none_body: A cutover adds an entry here: the fingerprint that took over, and the position it took over at.

done.cutover: {name} now answers the new version. The replaced one is kept for the rollback window.
done.finish: The replacement of {name} is finished and the replaced version has been released. There is no rollback now.
done.abandon: The replacement of {name} has been abandoned and the candidate released. The running version never stopped.
done.pause: The backfill of {name} is paused. What it has read is kept.
done.resume: The backfill of {name} is reading again.
done.throttle: The backfill now reads at most {rate} records a second.

error.rate: “{rate}” is not a number of records a second.
